target: Agent 1’s claim that dissection is mainly a productive reuse of already-dead animals rather than a driver of harm
objection: School dissection animal supply is not just leftover byproducts: approximately 99% of animals used for school dissection are caught in the wild, and that wild-catching decreases local populations and biodiversity.

target: Agent 1’s ethical framing of dissection as acceptable so long as the animals were already dead
objection: Even if some specimens are dead by the time they reach classrooms, the sourcing methods used for dissection animals are still inhumane and environmentally harmful, so dissection is ethically problematic.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that animal dissection is necessary for required biology or medical education
objection: Animal dissection is not required by AP Biology, NGSS, or physician-training programs in the U.S. and Canada, so it is not necessary to meet required educational outcomes.

target: Agent 1’s view that dissection is educationally necessary because alternatives are inferior
objection: Synthetic models and computer simulations teach anatomy and biology as well as or better than dissection, so students can learn the relevant material without using real animals.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection demand mostly drives wild-capture and biodiversity loss
objection: The stance says over 98% of dissected animals were already deceased and fetal pigs are meat-industry byproducts destined for landfills, so school dissection is mostly supplied by existing dead byproducts rather than by live wild-capture.

target: Agent 1’s response that dissection specimens are mostly byproducts and thus not environmentally harmful
objection: Even if some specimens are byproducts, the broader dissection supply chain still relies heavily on wild-caught animals, so the environmental objection remains relevant.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that dissection can proceed whenever a class is otherwise acceptable
objection: School dissections commonly involve preserved tissues and chemical or biohazard waste, which creates realistic safety risks unless proper PPE, ventilation, and waste controls are reliably in place.

target: Agent 1’s claim that safety concerns are overstated or can be ignored
objection: There is evidence that school lab practices often fall short on safety controls such as PPE, ventilation, and waste handling, so some dissection classes are unsafe or violate required safety standards.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives can fully replace dissection’s educational value
objection: Dissection teaches students to handle real specimens and follow lab safety protocols, so it also develops practical lab-safety competence that synthetic models and computer simulations do not provide in the same way.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection is unnecessary because alternatives are available
objection: Alternatives depend on having the right technology and materials, and many schools lack consistent access to high-quality simulations or models, so dissection can be the only feasible way to provide hands-on anatomy learning in some settings.

target: Agent 1’s broader claim that byproduct sourcing makes dissection ethically acceptable
objection: Typical school dissection supply chains still rely on inhumane wild-capture, so dissection is not merely using harmless byproducts.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that required ethical standards are satisfied if classroom procedures are supervised
objection: Required ethical standards for animal use include humane treatment and minimizing harm, so if animals are sourced through inhumane wild-capture, the class violates those standards regardless of classroom supervision.

target: Agent 2’s claim that alternatives can reproduce the same learning as dissection
objection: Dissection gives students tactile, three-dimensional understanding of real anatomical relationships by letting them physically cut and trace structures through actual tissue, which models and simulations cannot reproduce identically.

target: Agent 2’s claim that dissection does not provide distinctive inquiry skills
objection: Dissection trains scientific inquiry by requiring students to make direct observations, measurements, records, and inferences from real specimens, which is a core biology skill set.

target: Agent 1’s reliance on AP/NGSS non-requirement as a defense of dissection
objection: Because dissection provides no required, unique educational benefit and animal sourcing causes harm, the absence of a curriculum mandate does not justify requiring it.

target: Agent 1’s claim that the harms are overstated because the animals are mostly already dead
objection: Typical school dissection is still supplied through wild-caught animals and inhumane methods, so it creates real animal-welfare and biodiversity harms rather than being a harmless use of dead byproducts.

target: Agent 1’s assumption that ethical problems arise only if a specific class is unsafe
objection: Using inhumane wild-capture in the supply chain itself violates ethical animal-use standards, so the ethical problem exists even apart from classroom safety issues.

target: Agent 1’s weak-negation exception that a class is only objectionable if there is evidence of unsafe or unethical conditions
objection: Evidence that roughly 99% of dissection animals are wild-caught and that the sourcing is inhumane already satisfies the condition that a class violates required ethical/safety standards.

target: Agent 1’s claim that byproduct sourcing substantially reduces harm enough to justify dissection
objection: Because the dissection supply chain still commonly uses wild-captured animals and inhumane methods, the relevant sourcing harms are not substantially eliminated just by pointing to some byproduct specimens.

target: Agent 1’s idea that byproduct sourcing plus educational value is enough to justify dissection
objection: If school dissection depends on sourcing animals through inhumane methods, then it violates required ethical standards, so educational value does not override that problem.
